# Hotfix Daily: full text for LLMs

> Hotfix Daily is a free weekday email for people who build with AI: five things worth your attention in AI, AI agents, vibe coding, and game dev, plus one tip to try today. About a 3-minute read.
> Website: https://hotfixdaily.com/ · Subscribe: https://hotfixdaily.com/#subscribe

## The best AI coding agents for builders (October 2026)
URL: https://hotfixdaily.com/guides/ai-coding-agents/ · Last reviewed: 2026-10-21

Coding agents now live in three places: inside your editor, in your terminal, and in the cloud working on your repo while you do something else. Most builders end up using one from each group. Below is what each tool is (from its own docs), plus our take on who it suits. We left out pricing because it changes monthly; check each link before you pay.

### In your editor (IDE agents)
- **Cursor** (Desktop editor, plus CLI) <https://cursor.com>: An AI code editor built around agents you hand tasks to. Its docs cover Agent mode, Rules, Skills, MCP servers and a CLI. Our take: Builders who want one editor where agents do most of the typing. Source: https://cursor.com/docs
- **GitHub Copilot** (Editor, terminal, desktop and GitHub.com) <https://github.com/features/copilot>: GitHub's coding agent works from an open issue through to reviewing and merging a pull request, and runs in your editor, the terminal, a desktop app and on GitHub itself. Our take: Teams already living in GitHub issues and PRs. Source: https://github.com/features/copilot
- **Devin Desktop (formerly Windsurf)** (Desktop IDE plus cloud agents) <https://devin.ai/desktop>: Cognition renamed Windsurf to Devin Desktop on June 2, 2026. It keeps the full IDE and adds an Agent Command Center for managing local and cloud agents from one place. Our take: Windsurf users, and anyone who wants local and cloud agents in one window. Source: https://devin.ai/blog/windsurf-is-now-devin-desktop
- **Kiro** (Agentic IDE (from AWS)) <https://kiro.dev>: Kiro turns prompts into executable specs, checks code correctness, and runs parallel agents across large codebases. It is built by Amazon Web Services. Our take: Builders who like to plan with a written spec before code gets generated. Source: https://kiro.dev
- **Cline** (Open source (Apache-2.0): IDE extension, CLI or SDK) <https://cline.bot>: An open-source coding agent with Plan and Act modes and MCP support. You bring your own model provider. Our take: People who want an open-source agent and full control over which model they pay for. Source: https://github.com/cline/cline

### In your terminal (CLI agents)
- **Claude Code** (Terminal and IDE (Anthropic)) <https://www.claude.com/product/claude-code>: Anthropic's agentic coding tool understands your codebase, edits files and runs commands. It reads project instructions from CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md files. Our take: Long, multi-step changes in an existing codebase. Source: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory
- **Codex** (Open-source CLI (Apache-2.0), IDE extension, desktop app, cloud) <https://github.com/openai/codex>: OpenAI's coding agent runs locally in your terminal and can be scripted in CI with codex exec. There is also an IDE extension, a desktop app (macOS since Feb 2, 2026; Windows since Mar 4, 2026) and a cloud version. Usage is included in paid ChatGPT plans. Our take: ChatGPT subscribers, and anyone who wants to run agents in CI pipelines. Source: https://openai.com/index/introducing-the-codex-app/
- **Gemini CLI** (Open source (Apache-2.0) terminal agent) <https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli>: An open-source AI agent that brings Google's Gemini models into your terminal. Our take: Trying a terminal agent with Google's models, or forking one. Source: https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli
- **OpenCode** (Open source (MIT) terminal agent) <https://opencode.ai>: An open-source coding agent you can point at the model provider of your choice. Our take: Open-source fans who want a model-agnostic terminal agent. Source: https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode
- **Aider** (Open source (Apache-2.0) terminal pair programmer) <https://aider.chat>: AI pair programming in your terminal, working directly on your git repo. Our take: Small, focused edits with a clean git history. Source: https://github.com/Aider-AI/aider
- **Amp** (CLI and cloud runner) <https://ampcode.com>: A coding agent and development environment. You can run it on your own machine with its CLI, or unattended in the cloud. Our take: Builders who want to hand off long tasks and check back later. Source: https://ampcode.com

### In the cloud (async agents)
- **Jules** (Cloud agent (Google) connected to GitHub) <https://jules.google>: Clones your repo into a cloud VM, plans and makes the change, runs tests and can open a pull request. You can trigger it from GitHub or a GitHub Action. Our take: Clearing small issues and chores without tying up your laptop. Source: https://github.com/google-labs-code/jules-action
- **Devin** (Cloud agents (Cognition)) <https://devin.ai>: An autonomous AI software engineer that runs parallel cloud agents, aimed at engineering teams. Our take: Teams with a big backlog of well-scoped tickets. Source: https://devin.ai
- **Codex cloud and Copilot on GitHub** (Cloud) <https://github.com/features/copilot>: Both OpenAI (chatgpt.com/codex) and GitHub let you delegate a task in the browser and review the result as a diff or PR. Our take: Whoever already pays for ChatGPT or Copilot: try these before buying anything new. Source: https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/concepts/copilot-surfaces/copilot-on-github

FAQ:
- Q: What is an AI coding agent?
  A: A tool that doesn't just suggest code: it reads your project, makes changes across files, runs commands like tests, and reports back. You review and approve the result.
- Q: Which AI coding agent is best?
  A: There isn't one winner. Editor agents suit hands-on work, terminal agents suit larger changes and automation, and cloud agents suit backlog chores. Most builders use one from two of these groups.
- Q: Are there free or open-source coding agents?
  A: Yes. Cline, OpenCode, Aider, Gemini CLI and OpenAI's Codex CLI publish their source code on GitHub under open-source licenses. You still pay for model usage unless you run a local model.
- Q: What happened to Windsurf?
  A: Cognition renamed Windsurf to Devin Desktop on June 2, 2026. The IDE, plans and settings carried over.

## Which AI coding agent should you use? A pick-by-budget guide (October 2026)
URL: https://hotfixdaily.com/guides/which-ai-coding-agent/ · Last reviewed: 2026-10-21

The quickest way to pick a coding agent is to start with what you already pay for. ChatGPT, Claude, Google AI and GitHub plans now come with a coding agent, so many builders have one already. Below are the free options and the cheapest paid tiers for each agent, taken from the vendors' own pricing pages, then our take on which one suits which job. For what each tool actually does, read our AI coding agents guide.

### You already pay for a chat subscription
- **Codex: included with ChatGPT** (ChatGPT Free and Go ($8) for light tasks · Plus $20 · Pro $100, $200 or $500 · Business $20/user (billed annually, 2+ users; $25 monthly)) <https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/pricing>: OpenAI's pricing page says Codex is included in ChatGPT Free, Go, Plus, Pro, Business, Edu and Enterprise plans. Free is pitched for "quick coding tasks" and Go ($8) for "lightweight coding tasks"; both plan cards list a model in the desktop app, subject to rollout. Plus ($20) adds Codex on the web, in the CLI, in the IDE extension and on iOS, plus cloud integrations like automatic code review and Slack. Pro comes in $100, $200 and $500 tiers. You can also run Codex with an API key and pay API rates, which OpenAI calls great for automation like CI, but API-key use has no cloud features such as GitHub code review. Our take: ChatGPT subscribers, and anyone who wants to script an agent in CI. Source: https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/pricing
- **Claude Code: included with Claude Pro and Max** (Not on Free · Pro $20/month ($17/month billed annually) · Max from $100) <https://claude.com/pricing>: Anthropic's plan table lists Claude Code on Pro, Max 5x and Max 20x, but not on the Free plan. Pro costs $20 billed monthly, or $17 a month billed annually ($200 up front). Max starts at $100 a month with 5x or 20x Pro's usage, and Anthropic says Max includes $100 to $200 a month in API credits for building on the Claude Platform. On the Team plan, standard seats are $20 per seat a month billed annually ($25 monthly), and Claude Code is part of the Team plan. Our take: Long, multi-step changes in an existing codebase, if you already use Claude. Source: https://claude.com/pricing
- **Jules: included with Google AI plans** (Free: 15 tasks a day, 3 at once · Google AI Pro: 100 a day · Google AI Ultra: 300 a day) <https://jules.google/docs/usage-limits/>: Jules's docs list three plans. Free allows 15 tasks in a rolling 24 hours, with 3 running at once. "Jules in Pro" (part of Google AI Pro) allows 100 tasks and 15 at once. "Jules in Ultra" allows 300 tasks and 60 at once. The docs say paid Jules plans currently work only with individual Google accounts ending in @gmail.com. Our take: Clearing small issues for free while you work on something else. Source: https://jules.google/docs/usage-limits/

### The cheapest way to a paid editor agent
- **GitHub Copilot** (Free · Pro $10 · Pro+ $39 · Max $100) <https://github.com/features/copilot/plans>: GitHub's plans page lists Free at $0, Pro at $10, Pro+ at $39 and Max at $100 a month. The Free plan includes agent mode in VS Code, Visual Studio, JetBrains, Eclipse and Xcode, the Copilot CLI and MCP support, with limited chat and agent usage; GitHub says Free users are limited to 2,000 completions a month. Pro adds the cloud agent (assign work to Copilot and it creates a pull request) and pull request code review. Pro+ and Max add delegating tasks to third-party coding agents such as Claude and OpenAI Codex, which GitHub marks as a preview. Agent mode, code review, the cloud agent and the CLI all use GitHub AI Credits. Our take: The cheapest paid plan here that includes a cloud agent, especially for teams that already work in GitHub. Source: https://github.com/features/copilot/plans
- **Cursor** (Free · Plus $8 · Premium $30 · Super $100 · Ultra $200 · Teams from $30/user) <https://cursor.com/pricing>: Cursor's pricing page now shows individual plans that share one AI usage pool between Cursor and Grok, and the allowance refreshes weekly. Free has limited agent requests. Plus ($8) includes Grok models only. Premium ($30, 4x Plus's usage) adds cloud agents and automations, Bugbot AI code reviews, code hosting, and third-party models at API list price, billed separately by usage. Super ($100) and Ultra ($200) give 15x and 50x Plus's usage. Cursor itself recommends Premium for new AI users and Super for daily agent users, and says Plus is aimed at social creators with limited AI usage. Our take: Builders who want one editor where agents do most of the typing. If you want non-Grok models, budget for third-party usage on top of the plan. Source: https://cursor.com/pricing
- **Devin Desktop (formerly Windsurf)** (Free · Pro $20 · Max $200 · Teams $80/month plus $40 per full seat) <https://devin.ai/pricing>: Cognition's pricing page lists Free (a light agent quota, limited models, unlimited Tab completions and inline edits), Pro at $20 with higher quotas, frontier models and Devin Cloud agents, and Max at $200 with significantly higher quotas. Paid plans include an allowance that refreshes daily and weekly; after that you buy extra usage at API pricing. Windsurf was renamed Devin Desktop on June 2, 2026. Our take: Ex-Windsurf users, and anyone who wants local and cloud agents in one app for $20. Source: https://devin.ai/pricing, https://devin.ai/blog/windsurf-is-now-devin-desktop
- **Kiro** (Free (50 credits) · Pro $20 (1,000 credits) · Pro+ $40 (2,000) · Pro Max $100 (5,000) · Power $200 (10,000)) <https://kiro.dev/pricing/>: Kiro's pricing page lists a perpetual Free tier with 50 credits and access to Claude Sonnet 4.5 and open-weight models, with limits. Paid tiers run from Pro at $20 (1,000 credits) to Power at $200 (10,000 credits), and add-on credits cost $0.04 each. Kiro is built by AWS, and its big idea is turning a prompt into a written spec before it writes code. Our take: Builders who want to plan a feature in writing first, and AWS users. Source: https://kiro.dev/pricing/

### Free and open source: pay only for the model
- **Cline** (Free extension and CLI · usage-based model costs, or bring your own key) <https://cline.bot/pricing>: Cline says its open-source extension is completely free for individual developers. You pay only for AI inference, either through the Cline provider or with your own API keys from providers like Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, OpenRouter, AWS Bedrock and others. Enterprise is a separate paid offering. Our take: Full control over which model you pay for, inside your editor. Source: https://cline.bot/pricing
- **OpenCode and Aider** (Free, open source (OpenCode: MIT; Aider: Apache-2.0) · bring your own model) <https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode>: Both are open-source terminal agents you point at the model provider of your choice. Aider works directly on your git repo. Our take: Terminal users who want no subscription at all. Source: https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode, https://github.com/Aider-AI/aider
- **Gemini CLI** (Free, open source (Apache-2.0) · sign in with Google, or use a Gemini API key for usage-based billing) <https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli>: Google's open-source terminal agent. Its README lists three ways to sign in: your Google account, a Gemini API key (usage-based billing, with higher limits when you upgrade), or Vertex AI for enterprise teams. The README doesn't list free-tier quotas, so check them after you sign in. Our take: Trying a terminal agent for free on Google's models. Source: https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli

### Hand it off to the cloud
- **Amp** (Free Hobby tier · Individual from $20/month · Enterprise custom) <https://ampcode.com/docs/pricing>: Amp's pricing page says the free Hobby tier includes every product feature: you bring your own keys or link your ChatGPT or Claude subscription, self-hosted orbs are free, and Amp-hosted orbs are pay-as-you-go. The $20 Individual tier includes 45,000 minutes of hosted orb time. Amp says it adds no markup to providers' API prices for individuals and non-enterprise workspaces. Our take: Handing off long tasks to hosted runs and checking back later. Source: https://ampcode.com/docs/pricing
- **Copilot cloud agent, Codex cloud, Devin Cloud and Jules** (): You may already have a cloud agent. GitHub's cloud agent comes with Copilot Pro and up, Codex on the web with ChatGPT Plus and up, Devin Cloud with Devin Pro, and Jules has a free tier (all covered above). Our take: Start with low-risk issues and review every pull request.

### Game devs
If you work in Unity, your choice of agent matters less than you might think. Unity offers an official plugin for Claude Code, Codex and Grok, plus a Unity CLI with an MCP server. Unity's FAQ says the CLI, the MCP server and the plugin are all free to use with no concurrency limits. Only Unity's in-editor assistant uses credits, and for Personal users its free trial converts to a $10/month subscription. So pick the agent you already pay for and connect it to the Editor. Unreal and Roblox options are in our AI game dev tools guide.

### Pick by budget (our take)
- $0: GitHub Copilot Free in your editor, plus Gemini CLI or Jules Free for terminal and cloud tasks. If you have API credits, use Cline, OpenCode or Aider.
- $8 to $10: Cursor Plus ($8, Grok models only) or ChatGPT Go ($8, Codex for lightweight tasks) are the cheapest paid plans here. Copilot Pro ($10) is the cheapest that includes a cloud agent that opens pull requests.
- About $20: Pick the ecosystem you already use. ChatGPT Plus gets you Codex, Claude Pro gets you Claude Code, Devin Pro and Kiro Pro are $20, and Amp's Individual tier is from $20.
- $100 to $200 (all-day agent use): Claude Max, ChatGPT Pro, Copilot Max, Cursor Super or Ultra, Kiro Pro Max or Power, or Devin Max. Only move up once you're hitting your limits every week.
- Teams: Compare per-seat prices on each vendor's team plan. Claude Team, ChatGPT Business, Cursor Teams and Devin Teams list them on the pages linked above.

FAQ:
- Q: Which AI coding agent should I use?
  A: Start with the one that comes with a subscription you already pay for (Codex with ChatGPT, Claude Code with Claude Pro, Jules with Google AI). If you have none, GitHub Copilot has a free plan, and Copilot Pro at $10 a month is the cheapest plan here with a cloud agent. Our take: move to a pricier agent only when you hit its limits or need a workflow it lacks.
- Q: What's the cheapest AI coding agent?
  A: Several are free. Copilot Free, Jules Free (15 tasks a day), Kiro Free (50 credits), Devin Desktop Free and Cursor Free all have limited free plans. Cline, OpenCode, Aider and Gemini CLI are open source, so you pay only for model usage. The cheapest paid plans in this guide are Cursor Plus and ChatGPT Go at $8 a month, then Copilot Pro at $10.
- Q: Is Claude Code free?
  A: No. Anthropic's plan table lists Claude Code on Pro ($20 a month, or $17 a month billed annually) and Max (from $100), not on the Free plan.
- Q: Is Codex free?
  A: OpenAI says Codex is included in ChatGPT Free for quick coding tasks. Codex on the web, in the CLI, in the IDE extension and its cloud integrations are listed from Plus ($20). You can also pay API rates with an API key.
- Q: Do I need more than one coding agent?
  A: Not to start. Our take: many builders end up with one in the editor and one in the terminal or cloud, but one agent and a good review habit get you further than three agents. See our AI coding agents guide for how each type works.
- Q: Why is Cursor's pricing tied to Grok?
  A: Cursor's pricing page shows individual plans that share one usage pool across Cursor and Grok, and the plans also bundle Grok and X features. The $8 Plus plan includes Grok models only; on Premium and above, other providers' models are available at API list price, billed separately. Check the page for the current details.

## Vibe coding tools: build apps by describing them (October 2026)
URL: https://hotfixdaily.com/guides/vibe-coding-tools/ · Last reviewed: 2026-10-21

"Vibe coding" means describing what you want in plain language and letting an AI write the code. Andrej Karpathy coined the term in February 2025, and Merriam-Webster listed it as trending slang a month later. Today there are two kinds of vibe coding tools: browser app builders that host everything for you, and coding agents that work on real code on your machine. This guide covers the first kind and tells you when to move to the second.

### Browser app builders
- **Lovable** (Web apps and sites) <https://lovable.dev>: Describe what you want in plain language and Lovable builds it with you in real time. It also handles hosting, SSL, authentication, backend and payments. Our take: Non-developers shipping a real web product or internal tool. Source: https://lovable.dev
- **Bolt** (Websites, apps and prototypes) <https://bolt.new>: An AI builder that creates websites and apps from your words. Our take: Fast prototypes you can tweak in the browser. Source: https://bolt.new
- **v0 by Vercel** (Full-stack web apps) <https://v0.app>: Vercel's AI assistant for designing, iterating on and scaling full-stack web apps. Our take: Polished web UI, especially if you already deploy on Vercel. Source: https://v0.app
- **Replit** (Apps and websites, in the browser) <https://replit.com>: Describe what you want and Replit builds a working app or website. No coding required. Our take: Learners, and builders who want to go from idea to deployed app in one place. Source: https://replit.com
- **Base44** (No-code apps and websites (part of Wix)) <https://base44.com>: A no-code AI platform that turns ideas into working apps and websites. The site's footer shows it is owned by Wix.com Ltd. Our take: Simple business apps and dashboards with no code at all. Source: https://base44.com
- **Rork** (Mobile apps (iOS, Android) and web) <https://rork.com>: A cross-platform AI app builder that can publish to the App Store and Google Play. Our take: Getting a phone app into the stores without learning Swift or Kotlin. Source: https://rork.com
- **Firebase Studio** (Web-based full-stack workspace (Google)) <https://firebase.studio>: A browser-based workspace for full-stack app development with Gemini built in and app previews running on cloud emulators. Our take: Builders already on Firebase or Google Cloud. Source: https://firebase.studio

FAQ:
- Q: What is vibe coding?
  A: Building software by describing what you want in natural language and letting an AI model generate the code, often without reading every line. Andrej Karpathy coined the term in February 2025.
- Q: What's the best vibe coding tool for beginners?
  A: Our take: start with a browser builder (Lovable, Bolt, v0 or Replit) because hosting is handled for you. Pick by output: Rork for mobile apps, v0 for polished web UI, Lovable or Base44 for full apps with logins and data.
- Q: Is vibe-coded software safe to launch?
  A: It can be, but only if you review it like any other code: secrets, authentication and database permissions especially. Use the checklist on this page before real users sign up.

## The vibe coding workflow: from idea to shipped app (October 2026)
URL: https://hotfixdaily.com/guides/vibe-coding-workflow/ · Last reviewed: 2026-10-21

Getting a first version out of a vibe coding tool is easy. Getting it to the point where strangers can sign up, pay and trust it with their data takes more work. This guide walks through that one step at a time and names the feature or tool that handles each step, based on each tool's own docs. Haven't picked a builder yet? Start with our vibe coding tools guide, then come back.

### Step 1: Plan before you prompt
- **Lovable Plan mode** () <https://docs.lovable.dev/features/plan-mode>: Lovable's project chat has Chat, Plan and Build modes. In Plan mode, Lovable investigates and writes a plan you can edit and approve, and Lovable says Plan mode never modifies your code. It often asks clarifying questions first, and each Plan mode message costs one credit plus the cost of any subagent research. Our take: Any change that touches several screens or your data model. Source: https://docs.lovable.dev/features/plan-mode
- **Kiro specs** () <https://kiro.dev/docs/specs/>: Kiro turns an idea into three files: requirements.md (user stories and acceptance criteria), design.md (technical architecture and sequence diagrams) and tasks.md (an implementation plan split into discrete tasks). Our take: Writing a spec that any builder or agent can follow, even if you build somewhere else. Source: https://kiro.dev/docs/specs/
- **Replit Plan mode** () <https://replit.com/pricing>: Replit's pricing page lists Plan mode in its Core plan ($20 a month, or $18 billed annually). Our take: Replit users: plan first, then let Agent build. Source: https://replit.com/pricing

### Step 2: Build the first version
- **Lovable** () <https://lovable.dev>: Lovable hosts your app and includes a built-in backend with a database, authentication, storage, edge functions and AI. Source: https://docs.lovable.dev/features/cloud
- **Bolt** () <https://bolt.new>: Bolt's free plan includes 1M tokens a month (with a 300K daily limit), website hosting and unlimited databases. Pro is $18 a month billed annually and adds your own domain with no Bolt branding. Source: https://bolt.new/pricing
- **v0 by Vercel** () <https://v0.app>: v0's free plan deploys apps to Vercel and syncs with GitHub, with a 7-message-a-day limit. Source: https://v0.app/pricing
- **Replit Agent** () <https://replit.com>: In Replit's words, Agent "sets up your project, creates applications, checks its work, and fixes problems along the way." Source: https://docs.replit.com/features/agent/overview

### Step 3: Add data and logins safely
- **Lovable Cloud (built-in backend)** () <https://docs.lovable.dev/features/cloud>: Lovable's built-in backend gives you a database, real-time updates, user authentication, storage, edge functions, secrets and logs, with no separate setup. Lovable says it is built on Supabase's open-source foundation. You can also connect an external backend you set up yourself. Our take: Non-developers who want logins and data without leaving the builder. Source: https://docs.lovable.dev/features/cloud
- **Supabase Auth** () <https://supabase.com/docs/guides/auth>: Supabase Auth supports password, magic link, one-time password (OTP), social login and single sign-on (SSO). Our take: Any builder or coding agent that uses Supabase as the backend. Source: https://supabase.com/docs/guides/auth
- **Row Level Security (the step people skip)** () <https://supabase.com/docs/guides/database/postgres/row-level-security>: Supabase's docs put it plainly: a table in an exposed schema without RLS is readable and writable by any role with a grant on it, so enable RLS on every table in an exposed schema. They also warn that a policy reading to anon using ( true ) gives every unauthenticated visitor read access, so use it only for data that is meant to be public. Our take: Before launch, ask your builder or agent to list every table and its RLS policies, and read that list yourself. Source: https://supabase.com/docs/guides/database/postgres/row-level-security

### Step 4: Get your code into GitHub
- **Lovable to GitHub** () <https://docs.lovable.dev/integrations/github>: Lovable can export your project and keep it in two-way sync with github.com, GitHub Enterprise Cloud or GitHub Enterprise Server, for backup, collaboration and deployment. On paid plans you can also download the codebase directly. Source: https://docs.lovable.dev/integrations/github
- **Bolt to GitHub** () <https://support.bolt.new/integrations/git>: Connecting GitHub backs up your Bolt project with a full history of changes and syncs commits automatically. Each branch has its own memory. Because the code lives in GitHub, you can publish with Bolt hosting, the Netlify integration or another service. Source: https://support.bolt.new/integrations/git
- **v0 to GitHub** () <https://v0.app/docs/github>: A v0 chat connected to GitHub starts from the base branch you pick. When v0 has a change, it creates a working branch from that base and pushes there, and you ship through pull requests and CI. Source: https://v0.app/docs/github
- **Moving between builders** () <https://docs.replit.com/build/import-from-providers>: Replit can import a GitHub repository, including projects exported from Lovable, Bolt or Base44, so GitHub sync also lets you change builders without starting over. Source: https://docs.replit.com/build/import-from-providers

### Step 5: Keep building with a coding agent
- **AGENTS.md** () <https://agents.md>: An open format that its site calls "a README for agents": one place for the setup, build, test and code style commands that coding agents read. Add it to the repo before the agent's first task. Our take: If the builder still syncs with the repo, have the agent work on a branch so the builder and the agent don't overwrite each other. Source: https://agents.md

### Step 6: Test like a user
- **Playwright MCP** () <https://github.com/microsoft/playwright-mcp>: An MCP server that lets an agent drive a browser through Playwright using structured accessibility snapshots instead of screenshots. Microsoft notes that coding agents increasingly favor its Playwright CLI with skills because it uses fewer tokens, and keeps MCP for long-running, stateful browser sessions. Our take: Having an agent click through sign-up, login, password reset and checkout on a preview URL. Source: https://github.com/microsoft/playwright-mcp
- **Chrome DevTools MCP** () <https://github.com/ChromeDevTools/chrome-devtools-mcp>: Gives coding agents control of a live Chrome browser for debugging: analyze network requests, check console messages, record performance traces and take screenshots. Our take: Finding why a page is slow or why a request fails. Source: https://github.com/ChromeDevTools/chrome-devtools-mcp
- **Lovable security scans** () <https://docs.lovable.dev/features/security>: Lovable has two built-in scans. The Quick scan runs automatically every time you publish and checks database access rules, dependencies and more. The Deep scan also reviews your application code and runs on demand. Lovable can auto-fix eligible findings, and says the scans do not replace a thorough security review. Source: https://docs.lovable.dev/features/security

### Step 7: Take payments (in a sandbox first)
- **Stripe sandboxes and test cards** () <https://docs.stripe.com/testing>: In a Stripe sandbox, test card numbers simulate successful payments, declines, fraud, disputes, refunds and 3D Secure authentication, and no real money moves. You reach your sandboxes from the account picker in the Dashboard. Our take: Test at least one decline and one refund before you switch to live keys, and keep the secret key in server-side secrets, never in front-end code. Source: https://docs.stripe.com/testing

### Step 8: Ship it
- **v0 + Vercel** () <https://v0.app/docs/deployments>: v0 deploys to Vercel. Working branches get preview deployments for review, and publishing updates production. Source: https://v0.app/docs/deployments
- **Vercel from GitHub** () <https://vercel.com/docs/git>: Pushes get preview deployments, the production branch deploys to production, and Vercel offers instant rollback. Source: https://vercel.com/docs/git
- **Netlify** () <https://docs.netlify.com/deploy/create-deploys/>: Deploy from Git, the CLI, drag and drop, or AI agents, with Deploy Previews for review. Source: https://docs.netlify.com/deploy/create-deploys/

FAQ:
- Q: What is a vibe coding workflow?
  A: The steps for taking an app you built by describing it to an AI all the way to launch: plan, build, add data and logins, back up to GitHub, test, take payments and deploy. Vibe coding is fast at step 2. This workflow covers the other steps.
- Q: Can I ship a vibe-coded app to production?
  A: Yes, if you review it like any other code. Supabase says to enable RLS on every table in an exposed schema, Stripe sandboxes let you test payments without real money, and preview deployments let you check each change before it goes live.
- Q: How do I get my code out of Lovable, Bolt or v0?
  A: All three have GitHub integrations. Lovable has two-way sync, Bolt syncs commits automatically, and v0 pushes to a working branch that you merge through pull requests. Lovable's paid plans can also download the codebase.
- Q: When should I switch from a builder to a coding agent?
  A: Our take: when you need custom backend logic, keep hitting the builder's limits, or spend more on credits than a coding agent subscription. Sync to GitHub first so you don't start over.
- Q: Do I need to know how to code?
  A: Not for steps 1 to 4, or for step 8 on builder hosting. For steps 5 and 6 it helps to read diffs and test results, or to have someone who can.

## AI game dev tools in 2026: engines, assets, NPCs and prototyping
URL: https://hotfixdaily.com/guides/ai-game-dev-tools/ · Last reviewed: 2026-10-21

AI in game dev has moved from novelty generators into the engines themselves. Unity, Unreal and Roblox now all let AI agents act inside the editor, and the common plug is MCP (Model Context Protocol). Adoption is wide but shallow: in a Vivrato survey of 101 studio leaders, 94% use AI in at least one production stage, yet 52% rate how deeply it's integrated at 3 out of 10 or lower.

### AI inside the engine
- **Unity's AI tools** (Unity 6+) <https://unity.com/features/ai>: An agentic in-editor assistant, a free Unity CLI with an MCP server, and an official plugin for Claude Code, Codex and Grok. The CLI, MCP server and plugin are free. The in-editor assistant uses credits; Personal users get a free trial that converts to $10/month. Unity has retired the "Unity AI" brand name, and Muse is deprecated. Our take: Unity devs who want their existing coding agent to drive the Editor. Source: https://unity.com/features/ai
- **Unreal Engine MCP plugin** (Unreal Engine 5.8 (Experimental)) <https://www.unrealengine.com/news/state-of-unreal-2026-top-news-from-the-show>: UE 5.8 adds an Experimental Model Context Protocol plugin that connects models like Claude or Gemini directly to UE projects. Epic says UE6 will build in MCP integrations and is targeting Early Access at the end of 2027. Our take: Unreal teams ready to experiment with agents operating editor workflows. Source: https://www.unrealengine.com/news/state-of-unreal-2026-top-news-from-the-show
- **Roblox Assistant** (Roblox Studio) <https://create.roblox.com/docs/assistant/guide>: An AI helper in Studio that answers questions, creates and edits objects and scripts, inserts Creator Store assets, generates materials, and generates 3D meshes and procedural models. Our take: Roblox creators who want to automate repetitive Studio work. Source: https://create.roblox.com/docs/assistant/guide
- **Roblox Cube** (Open model on GitHub) <https://github.com/Roblox/cube>: Roblox's foundation model for 3D intelligence, published on GitHub. Our take: Technical teams researching 3D generation. Source: https://github.com/Roblox/cube

### Art, 3D and audio assets
- **Scenario** (Web platform) <https://www.scenario.com>: Brings leading AI models together for game assets and creative production, with workflows and agents for image, video, 3D and audio pipelines. Our take: Studios that want a consistent style across many generated assets. Source: https://www.scenario.com
- **Meshy** (Web platform) <https://www.meshy.ai>: An AI 3D model generator for text and images that exports FBX, OBJ, GLB and STL. Our take: Props and placeholder 3D models. Source: https://www.meshy.ai
- **Tripo** (Web platform) <https://www.tripo3d.ai>: Turns text or images into 3D models for games, 3D printing and animation. Our take: Quick 3D concepts from a sketch or reference image. Source: https://www.tripo3d.ai
- **Ludo.ai** (Web platform) <https://ludo.ai>: Generates game assets ready for your engine: sprites, icons, UI, textures, music, 3D and video. Our take: 2D and indie games that need many sprites and icons. Source: https://ludo.ai
- **ElevenLabs** (API and web app) <https://elevenlabs.io>: An AI voice generator and voice agents platform with APIs and SDKs. Our take: Placeholder or final voice-over, and talking characters. Source: https://elevenlabs.io

### Characters, NPCs and prototyping
- **Inworld AI** (API) <https://inworld.ai>: Realtime voice models and open LLMs for consumer apps, including games. Our take: Voiced, responsive characters with low latency. Source: https://inworld.ai
- **Convai** (API and engine plugins) <https://www.convai.com>: Conversational AI for games, XR and virtual worlds, used to bring characters to life. Our take: Talking NPCs in 3D worlds. Source: https://convai.com
- **Rosebud AI** (Browser game maker) <https://rosebud.ai>: Create playable games from prompts or templates, then build and deploy them. No coding required. Our take: Game jams, prototypes and non-coders. Source: https://rosebud.ai

FAQ:
- Q: Can AI build a game for me?
  A: Browser tools like Rosebud can make small playable games from prompts. For anything bigger, AI speeds up parts of the work (code, assets, voices) while you still design and integrate.
- Q: Does Unity still have Muse?
  A: No. Unity says Muse is deprecated. Its current AI tools are an in-editor assistant, a CLI with an MCP server, and an official plugin for coding agents.
- Q: Can I connect Claude or another agent to Unreal Engine?
  A: Yes, experimentally. Unreal Engine 5.8 added an Experimental MCP plugin that connects models like Claude or Gemini to UE projects.

## AI agent frameworks compared (October 2026)
URL: https://hotfixdaily.com/guides/ai-agent-frameworks/ · Last reviewed: 2026-10-21

A coding agent writes your code. An agent framework is what you reach for when the agent is your product: it runs the loop of model calls and tool calls, keeps state, and lets a human step in. Most of these now work with more than one model provider, so the real differences are language, how much control you get over each step, and which ecosystem you already use. Licenses below come from each project's GitHub repo. We left out stars and pricing because they change every week.

### SDKs from the model labs
- **OpenAI Agents SDK** (Python and TypeScript · MIT) <https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-python/>: OpenAI's lightweight framework for multi-agent workflows. Agents get instructions, tools, guardrails and handoffs, with built-in sessions, human-in-the-loop and tracing. It also covers realtime voice agents and sandbox agents that work inside a container. Its README says it is provider-agnostic: it supports OpenAI's Responses and Chat Completions APIs plus 100+ other LLMs. Our take: A small API with tracing built in, especially for voice agents. Source: https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python
- **Claude Agent SDK** (Python and TypeScript (Anthropic)) <https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/overview>: Anthropic describes it as Claude Code as a library. Your agent gets Claude Code's tools for reading and editing files and running commands, plus MCP, subagents, skills, hooks and permission controls. The Python package bundles the Claude Code CLI, so there is nothing else to install. It used to be called the Claude Code SDK. The Python repo is MIT-licensed; the docs link Anthropic's license and terms. Our take: Agents that work on files and code: internal dev tools, research bots, ops agents. Source: https://github.com/anthropics/claude-agent-sdk-python
- **Google Agent Development Kit (ADK)** (Python, TypeScript, Java, Go, Kotlin · Apache-2.0) <https://adk.dev/>: Google's open-source, code-first toolkit, now at version 2.0 in Python. It adds a graph-based workflow runtime (routing, fan-out, loops, retries, human-in-the-loop), structured agent-to-agent delegation, and MCP and OpenAPI tools. It is optimized for Gemini but model-agnostic, and deploys to Cloud Run or Vertex AI Agent Engine. Our take: Teams on Gemini or Google Cloud, or anyone who wants one framework across several languages. Source: https://github.com/google/adk-python
- **Strands Agents** (Python and TypeScript · Apache-2.0) <https://strandsagents.com/>: An open-source SDK for building and running agents inside your own process, with no hosted control plane. It supports Amazon Bedrock, Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini and other providers. The repo (now strands-agents/harness-sdk) also ships a ready-made harness agent, a CLI, and plugins for Claude Code, Codex and Cursor. Our take: Builders who would otherwise hand-roll their own agent loop, especially on Bedrock. Source: https://github.com/strands-agents/harness-sdk

### Orchestration frameworks
- **LangGraph** (Python and JavaScript · MIT) <https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/overview>: LangChain's low-level orchestration framework for long-running, stateful agents. It offers durable execution that resumes where it left off after a failure, human-in-the-loop interrupts, and short- and long-term memory. For a quicker start, LangChain points to Deep Agents, a higher-level package built on LangGraph. Our take: Complex flows where you want to control every step and survive crashes. Source: https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph
- **CrewAI** (Python · MIT) <https://docs.crewai.com/>: An open-source Python framework with two layers: Crews, teams of role-based agents that collaborate, and Flows, event-driven workflows for precise control. A paid AMP Suite adds managed deployment, observability and governance. Our take: Getting a multi-agent team (researcher, writer, reviewer) working fast. Source: https://github.com/crewAIInc/crewAI
- **Microsoft Agent Framework** (.NET and Python (Go in a separate repo) · MIT) <https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/agent-framework/>: Microsoft's framework for production agents and multi-agent workflows, with graph-based patterns (sequential, concurrent, handoff, group collaboration), middleware, durability and observability. Version 1.0 is a production release with stable APIs, and Microsoft calls it the enterprise-ready successor to AutoGen. Our take: .NET shops, and teams on Azure or Microsoft Foundry. Source: https://github.com/microsoft/agent-framework

### TypeScript-first
- **AI SDK (Vercel)** (TypeScript · Apache-2.0) <https://ai-sdk.dev/docs/introduction>: A free, provider-agnostic TypeScript toolkit for AI apps and agents. It works with Next.js, React, Svelte, Vue, Angular and Node.js. By default it routes model names through Vercel AI Gateway, or you can install a provider package to connect directly. Our take: Adding an agent or chat feature to a web app you already ship. Source: https://github.com/vercel/ai
- **Mastra** (TypeScript · Apache-2.0 core, enterprise code separately licensed) <https://mastra.ai/docs>: A TypeScript framework for agents and AI apps: agents, a graph-based workflow engine, suspend-and-resume human-in-the-loop, memory, RAG, evals and observability, and routing to 40+ model providers through one interface. It can also publish your agents and tools as MCP servers. Our take: TypeScript teams who want workflows, memory and evals in one package. Source: https://github.com/mastra-ai/mastra

### Python-first and minimal
- **Pydantic AI** (Python · MIT) <https://pydantic.dev/docs/ai/overview/>: From the Pydantic team: a typed agent loop where switching models is a one-string change. Companion packages add a harness (memory, guardrails, sub-agents), evals that grade tool-call trajectories, and graphs. Our take: Python devs who want type-checked inputs and outputs and testable agents. Source: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic-ai
- **smolagents** (Python · Apache-2.0) <https://huggingface.co/docs/smolagents/index>: Hugging Face's minimal agent library: the core logic fits in about 1,000 lines. Its CodeAgent writes its actions as code, which you can run in sandboxes such as E2B, Modal, Blaxel or Docker. It works with any model, including local ones, and can use tools from MCP servers or the Hugging Face Hub. Our take: Learning how agents work, and experiments with open or local models. Source: https://github.com/huggingface/smolagents

FAQ:
- Q: What is an AI agent framework?
  A: A library for building software where a model decides which tools to call, in a loop, until a task is done. Frameworks handle the loop, tool calling, memory and state, and usually tracing and human approval steps.
- Q: Do I need an agent framework at all?
  A: Our take: not always. One model with a few tools works fine with a lab SDK or even a hand-written loop. Reach for an orchestration framework when runs are long, have many steps, need approvals, or must resume after a crash.
- Q: What happened to Microsoft AutoGen?
  A: Microsoft has put AutoGen in maintenance mode, limited to bug fixes, security patches and docs. It recommends new users start with Microsoft Agent Framework and publishes a migration guide.
- Q: Which agent frameworks support MCP?
  A: The OpenAI Agents SDK, Claude Agent SDK, Google ADK and smolagents all list MCP tools in their docs, and Mastra can publish agents and tools as MCP servers. Check each project's docs for the transports it supports.
- Q: What's the best agent framework for TypeScript?
  A: Our take: the AI SDK if you are adding AI features to a web app, Mastra if you want workflows, memory and evals in one package. The OpenAI Agents SDK, Claude Agent SDK, ADK, LangGraph and Strands also have TypeScript versions.

## MCP servers worth knowing for builders (October 2026)
URL: https://hotfixdaily.com/guides/mcp-servers/ · Last reviewed: 2026-10-21

MCP, the Model Context Protocol, is an open standard for connecting AI apps to outside tools and data. Its own docs call it a USB-C port for AI applications. Claude, ChatGPT, VS Code, Cursor and many other apps support it, and the current version of the spec is dated July 28, 2026. An MCP server is the plug-in side: it gives your agent tools like "open a pull request" or "query this table". Below are the servers we think are worth knowing, grouped by job, each described from its own docs.

### Code and project tools
- **GitHub MCP Server** (Hosted by GitHub, or run locally · MIT) <https://github.com/github/github-mcp-server>: GitHub's official server. Agents can browse and search code, manage issues and pull requests, check GitHub Actions runs and build failures, and review security findings and Dependabot alerts. The hosted version is at api.githubcopilot.com/mcp/. Our take: Any agent that needs to read or act on your repos. Source: https://github.com/github/github-mcp-server
- **Linear MCP server** (Hosted by Linear) <https://linear.app/docs/mcp>: Find, create and update Linear issues, projects and comments. Setup uses OAuth, and a read-only endpoint (mcp.linear.app/mcp/readonly) exposes only read tools. Our take: Letting your coding agent pick up and update tickets. Source: https://linear.app/docs/mcp
- **Sentry MCP** (Hosted by Sentry, or self-hosted) <https://mcp.sentry.dev/>: Built mainly for human-in-the-loop coding agents like Cursor and Claude Code. Its tools focus on developer debugging workflows rather than all of Sentry. Our take: Fixing production errors with the real stack trace in front of the agent. Source: https://github.com/getsentry/toolkit

### Browsers and testing
- **Playwright MCP** (Local (Node.js) · Apache-2.0) <https://github.com/microsoft/playwright-mcp>: Browser automation through Playwright using the page's accessibility tree instead of screenshots, so no vision model is needed. Microsoft notes that coding agents may use fewer tokens with its Playwright CLI and skills, and suggests MCP for long-running, stateful browser loops. Our take: Letting an agent click through your app to test a flow. Source: https://github.com/microsoft/playwright-mcp
- **Chrome DevTools MCP** (Local · Apache-2.0) <https://developer.chrome.com/docs/devtools/agents>: Lets a coding agent control and inspect a live Chrome browser: record performance traces, analyze network requests, read console messages with source-mapped stack traces, and take screenshots. It is also available as a CLI. Our take: Debugging front-end bugs and slow pages. Source: https://github.com/ChromeDevTools/chrome-devtools-mcp

### Up-to-date docs
- **Context7** (Hosted by Upstash, plus open-source server · MIT) <https://context7.com/>: Pulls current, version-specific library docs and code examples into your agent, so it stops guessing at old APIs. Codex's docs use it as their example of adding an MCP server. Our take: Fast-moving libraries that your model's training data is behind on. Source: https://github.com/upstash/context7

### Backend, payments and hosting
- **Supabase MCP server** (Hosted at mcp.supabase.com · Apache-2.0) <https://supabase.com/docs/guides/getting-started/mcp>: Connects an agent to your Supabase project to manage tables, fetch config and query data. Supabase asks you to read its security best practices first. The local Supabase CLI exposes a smaller set of tools. Our take: Vibe coders on Supabase who want the agent to set up the schema. Source: https://github.com/supabase/mcp
- **Stripe MCP server** (Hosted at mcp.stripe.com (public preview)) <https://docs.stripe.com/mcp>: Lets agents work with the Stripe API and search Stripe's docs and support articles. It connects with OAuth, and Stripe's agent plugins can set it up for you. Our take: Building and testing payment flows, ideally in test mode first. Source: https://docs.stripe.com/mcp
- **Cloudflare MCP servers** (Hosted by Cloudflare · Apache-2.0) <https://github.com/cloudflare/mcp-server-cloudflare>: Cloudflare runs several remote MCP servers. It recommends its Cloudflare API server (mcp.cloudflare.com/mcp) for broad API access, with separate servers for docs, sandbox containers and browser rendering. Some older servers are deprecated. Our take: Builders on Workers and Pages. Source: https://github.com/cloudflare/mcp-server-cloudflare

### Design and docs workspaces
- **Figma MCP server** (Hosted (recommended) or desktop app) <https://developers.figma.com/docs/figma-mcp-server/>: Gives agents design context to generate code from your Figma files, and can write native Figma content back to the canvas. Writing outside your drafts needs the remote server and a Full seat. Our take: Turning designs into front-end code that matches your design system. Source: https://developers.figma.com/docs/figma-mcp-server/
- **Notion MCP** (Hosted by Notion) <https://developers.notion.com/docs/mcp>: Notion's hosted server uses OAuth and your existing Notion permissions to search, read and edit pages in Markdown. Notion says its older self-hosted server is no longer actively maintained. Our take: Agents that read specs or write notes in your Notion workspace. Source: https://github.com/makenotion/notion-mcp-server

### Finding, testing and building servers
- **Official MCP Registry** (Web directory and API) <https://registry.modelcontextprotocol.io/>: The project's own list of published MCP servers, which it describes as an app store for MCP servers. It launched in preview in September 2025. Our take: Checking whether an official server exists before you install a random one. Source: https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/registry
- **MCP Inspector** (Web UI, CLI or terminal UI) <https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/inspector>: The official developer tool for inspecting MCP servers. Run npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector to list a server's tools and try them by hand. Our take: Seeing exactly what a server exposes before you give it to an agent. Source: https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/inspector
- **Reference servers** (Examples from the MCP steering group) <https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers>: A small set of reference servers (Everything, Fetch, Filesystem, Git, Memory, Sequential Thinking, Time). The repo says they are educational examples, not production-ready tools. Our take: Learning how to build your own server. Source: https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers

FAQ:
- Q: What is MCP (Model Context Protocol)?
  A: An open-source standard for connecting AI applications to external systems such as files, databases, tools and workflows. An app that supports MCP (the client) can use any MCP server, so a tool is built once and works in many agents.
- Q: Which apps support MCP?
  A: Claude, ChatGPT, Claude Code, Cursor, VS Code with Copilot and Codex all document MCP support, along with many other clients and agent frameworks.
- Q: What's the difference between a local and a remote MCP server?
  A: A local server runs on your machine, usually started by your agent with a command like npx. A remote server is hosted by the vendor at a URL and usually signs you in with OAuth. Many vendors, including GitHub, Linear, Stripe and Notion, now recommend their hosted servers.
- Q: Are MCP servers safe?
  A: They act with whatever access you give them, so treat them like any integration. Use official servers, read-only scopes and test accounts where you can, and review the tool list first. The MCP project publishes security best practices.
- Q: Is MCP being replaced by CLIs and skills?
  A: Not replaced, but some teams now suggest both. Microsoft's Playwright docs say coding agents increasingly favor a CLI plus skills because it uses fewer tokens, while MCP still suits long-running, stateful work.

## How to add an MCP server: Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, VS Code (2026)
URL: https://hotfixdaily.com/guides/how-to-add-mcp-servers/ · Last reviewed: 2026-10-21

You found an MCP server you want, maybe from our MCP servers worth knowing list. Now you need to plug it in. Every client does this a bit differently: Claude Code, Codex and Gemini CLI have an mcp add command, Cursor and VS Code use JSON files, and Codex stores its config in TOML. Below are the commands and file locations for each client, taken from their own docs, then how to test a server before your agent touches it and how to fix the usual problems.

### Before you start: local or remote?
- **How to tell which one you have** () <https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/learn/architecture>:  If the vendor gives you a URL (like https://mcp.notion.com/mcp), it's a remote HTTP server, and it usually signs you in with OAuth. If the vendor gives you a command (like npx -y @playwright/mcp@latest), it's a local stdio server, and you need its runtime, such as Node.js. SSE is the older remote transport. Claude Code's docs call it deprecated and say to use HTTP servers where available. Source: https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/learn/architecture, https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/modelcontextprotocol/releases

### Client by client
- **Claude Code** (claude mcp add · ~/.claude.json (local and user scopes) or .mcp.json at the project root (project scope)) <https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp>:  `# Remote (HTTP) server
claude mcp add --transport http notion https://mcp.notion.com/mcp

# Local (stdio) server: everything after -- goes to the server untouched
claude mcp add --env AIRTABLE_API_KEY=YOUR_KEY --transport stdio airtable \
  -- npx -y airtable-mcp-server

# Manage
claude mcp list
claude mcp get <name>
claude mcp remove <name>` Scopes: local is the default and private to you in that project. project writes .mcp.json so the whole team gets it through git. user is private to you and loads in every project. Add --scope project or --scope user to change it. Inside a session, /mcp shows status and handles OAuth sign-in. Already set up Claude Desktop? claude mcp add-from-claude-desktop imports its servers. Claude Code prompts for approval in interactive sessions before using project-scoped servers from .mcp.json. Its docs say claude -p runs and Agent SDK sessions load them without asking. Our take: Use project scope for servers that need no secrets, and local or user scope for anything that uses a token. Source: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp
- **Cursor** (Customize page or Cursor Marketplace · .cursor/mcp.json (project) or ~/.cursor/mcp.json (global)) <https://cursor.com/docs/mcp>:  Cursor supports stdio, SSE and Streamable HTTP, and remote servers can use OAuth. A local server uses command, args and env under mcpServers. A remote server uses url and optional headers. `{
  "mcpServers": {
    "my-remote": {
      "url": "https://api.example.com/mcp",
      "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer ${env:MY_TOKEN}" }
    }
  }
}` Cursor resolves ${env:NAME} in command, args, env, url and headers, so tokens stay out of the file. Cursor asks for approval before using MCP tools by default, and MCP follows the same Run Modes as terminal commands. Our take: Commit .cursor/mcp.json with ${env:...} references only, never with real keys. Source: https://cursor.com/docs/mcp
- **Codex (CLI, IDE extension and ChatGPT desktop app)** (codex mcp add · ~/.codex/config.toml, or .codex/config.toml in a trusted project) <https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/extend/mcp>:  `# Local (stdio) server
codex mcp add context7 -- npx -y @upstash/context7-mcp

# Remote server, then sign in if it uses OAuth
codex mcp add <name> --url https://mcp.example.com
codex mcp login <name>

codex mcp list` In TOML, each server is a [mcp_servers.<name>] table. Local servers use command, args and env; remote servers use url, and optionally bearer_token_env_var or http_headers. `[mcp_servers.figma]
url = "https://mcp.figma.com/mcp"
bearer_token_env_var = "FIGMA_OAUTH_TOKEN"
default_tools_approval_mode = "writes"
startup_timeout_sec = 20
tool_timeout_sec = 60` The ChatGPT desktop app, Codex CLI and IDE extension share this config. In the terminal UI, /mcp lists your active servers. Useful options: enabled_tools and disabled_tools (allow and deny lists), default_tools_approval_mode (auto, prompt, writes or approve), startup_timeout_sec (default 10) and tool_timeout_sec (default 60). Our take: Set default_tools_approval_mode = "writes" on servers that can change things, so Codex prompts for any tool that isn't marked read-only. Source: https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/extend/mcp
- **VS Code with GitHub Copilot** (Command Palette → MCP: Add Server · ~/.copilot/mcp-config.json (Global > Copilot) or a workspace-root .mcp.json) <https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/agent-customization/mcp-servers>:  The guided flow asks for a server URL (HTTP or SSE) or a launch command (stdio). It can also generate a config from an npm package, pip package or Docker image name, and shows the publisher for you to confirm first. A workspace-root .mcp.json needs the experimental chat.mcp.workspaceRootConfig.enabled setting. The older .vscode/mcp.json and user-profile mcp.json still work and are labeled deprecated in the guided flow. Format gotcha: portable files use a top-level mcpServers object, while the VS Code format uses servers. Check which one before you copy a config across. Our take: Copilot's Free plan already includes MCP in agent mode, so you can try all of this at no cost. Source: https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/agent-customization/mcp-servers, https://github.com/features/copilot/plans
- **Gemini CLI** (gemini mcp add · .gemini/settings.json (project, the default) or ~/.gemini/settings.json (user, with -s user)) <https://geminicli.com/docs/tools/mcp-server/>:  `gemini mcp add [options] <name> <commandOrUrl> [args...]

# Remote server over HTTP
gemini mcp add -t http my-server https://mcp.example.com/mcp

gemini mcp list` The transport defaults to stdio; use -t http or -t sse for remote servers. --include-tools and --exclude-tools limit which tools load, and --timeout sets the connection timeout in milliseconds. --trust bypasses all tool call confirmation prompts, so use it only for servers you fully trust. In settings.json, command is for stdio, url for SSE and httpUrl for Streamable HTTP. /mcp shows server status, and gemini mcp enable, disable and remove manage servers. Our take: Leave --trust off. The confirmation prompts are your safety net. Source: https://geminicli.com/docs/tools/mcp-server/
- **Cline** (MCP Servers icon → Configure (IDE), or ~/.cline/data/settings/cline_mcp_settings.json (CLI)) <https://docs.cline.bot/mcp/mcp-overview>:  In the IDE, the Remote Servers tab takes a name and URL, and offers Streamable HTTP (recommended) or SSE (legacy). In the JSON file, servers go under mcpServers. The CLI path can be changed with the CLINE_MCP_SETTINGS_PATH environment variable, and cline mcp opens a setup wizard. Source: https://docs.cline.bot/mcp/mcp-overview
- **Claude Desktop** (Settings → Developer → Edit Config · claude_desktop_config.json) <https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/develop/connect-local-servers>:  macOS: ~/Library/Application Support/Claude/claude_desktop_config.json. Windows: %APPDATA%\Claude\claude_desktop_config.json. The MCP docs walk through it with the Filesystem server. Logs are in ~/Library/Logs/Claude (macOS) or %APPDATA%\Claude\logs (Windows). Source: https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/develop/connect-local-servers

### Test and find servers
- **MCP Inspector** () <https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/inspector>: The official tool for inspecting MCP servers. List a server's tools and try them by hand before an agent gets them. `npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector        # web UI (default)
npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector --cli  # CLI
npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector --tui  # terminal UI` The README says it stores secrets such as OAuth tokens in the OS keychain by default. On machines with no keychain (headless Linux, SSH sessions, some containers) they go to ~/.mcp-inspector/secrets.json, unencrypted unless you supply a key. Our take: Seeing exactly what a server exposes, and checking whether a problem is the server or your client. Source: https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/inspector
- **Official MCP Registry** () <https://registry.modelcontextprotocol.io/>: The MCP project's list of published servers, which it describes as "like an app store for MCP servers." It launched in preview on September 8, 2025, and the project says it is still a preview release, so breaking changes or data resets may happen. Our take: Checking whether a vendor publishes an official server before you install a community one. Source: https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/registry

### Troubleshooting
- Server won't start in time. Claude Code: set MCP_TIMEOUT (for example MCP_TIMEOUT=10000 claude for 10 seconds). Codex: raise startup_timeout_sec (default 10). Gemini CLI: pass --timeout in milliseconds.
- Long tool calls time out. Claude Code accepts a per-server timeout in milliseconds in .mcp.json (for example "timeout": 600000 for ten minutes). Codex uses tool_timeout_sec (default 60).
- Remote server is skipped in Claude Code. A JSON entry with a url but no type is read as stdio and skipped. Add "type": "http"; Claude Code also accepts streamable-http as an alias.
- Tool output is cut off. Claude Code warns above 10,000 tokens of MCP output and limits it to 25,000 tokens by default. Raise the limit with MAX_MCP_OUTPUT_TOKENS.
- Config copied from another app doesn't load. Check the top-level key: mcpServers for most clients, servers for the VS Code format, and [mcp_servers.<name>] tables in Codex TOML.
- Still stuck? Connect the same server to MCP Inspector. If it works there, the problem is your client config.

### Safety settings worth turning on
- Only connect servers you trust. Claude Code's docs warn that servers which fetch external content can expose you to prompt injection.
- Load fewer tools. Use Codex enabled_tools or Gemini --include-tools so the agent sees only the tools it needs.
- Keep approvals on. Cursor asks before MCP tools by default, Codex can prompt on writes only, and Gemini's --trust should stay off for servers that can change things.
- Keep secrets out of shared files. Use ${env:NAME} in Cursor, bearer_token_env_var in Codex, or local and user scope in Claude Code.
- Read the spec's security guidance: MCP security best practices.

FAQ:
- Q: How do I add an MCP server?
  A: Find out whether the server is remote (a URL) or local (a command). Then use your client's add command (claude mcp add, codex mcp add, gemini mcp add), its UI (Cursor's Customize page, VS Code's MCP: Add Server), or its config file. Then check the server's status, for example with /mcp in Claude Code, Codex or Gemini CLI.
- Q: Where is the MCP config file?
  A: Claude Code: ~/.claude.json and project .mcp.json. Cursor: .cursor/mcp.json or ~/.cursor/mcp.json. Codex: ~/.codex/config.toml or project .codex/config.toml. VS Code: ~/.copilot/mcp-config.json or workspace .mcp.json. Gemini CLI: .gemini/settings.json or ~/.gemini/settings.json.
- Q: What's the difference between stdio and Streamable HTTP?
  A: Stdio runs the server as a local process on your machine. Streamable HTTP connects to a server at a URL and supports standard HTTP auth such as bearer tokens, API keys and headers; MCP recommends OAuth to get tokens. SSE is the older remote transport.
- Q: Can I use the same MCP config in every client?
  A: Not always as-is. Most clients use an mcpServers object, the VS Code format uses servers, and Codex uses TOML tables. The server itself works in any client that supports its transport.
- Q: How do I test an MCP server without an agent?
  A: Run npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector, connect to the server, and call its tools by hand.
- Q: Is it safe to commit .mcp.json?
  A: Yes, if it has no secrets. Use environment variable references or OAuth. Claude Code prompts for approval before using project-scoped servers in interactive sessions, but not in claude -p runs.

## Hotfix Daily #2: MiniMax M3.1 Flash, Claude Duet, Flint and more
URL: https://hotfixdaily.com/issues/002/ · Date: 2026-10-22



**Issue #2 · Thursday, Oct 22, 2026**

Five things from the last 48 hours worth your attention if you build with AI. No fluff.

[Read this issue on the web](https://hotfixdaily.com/issues/002/) · [Sponsor Hotfix Daily](https://hotfixdaily.com/sponsor/)

---

[MODEL]
**1. MiniMax ships M3.1 Flash at $0.15 per million input tokens**
MiniMax says its new Flash model runs agent tasks nearly 3x faster and about 70% cheaper than its predecessor, with a 1M-token context. Pricing is flat: $0.15 per million input tokens and $0.60 per million output. Weights are promised later.
*Why builders care:* If you tried the free `:free` variant on OpenRouter, it ends today at 12:00 UTC (7 AM CT). Switch to the base slug `minimax/minimax-m3.1-flash` so nothing breaks.
[source](https://www.minimax.io/blog/minimax-m31f)

[AGENTS]
**2. Anthropic previews Claude Duet, an agent that comes to you first**
Duet is a separate app (iOS, Android, claude.ai) that checks your connected apps every few hours, sends a morning brief, and keeps working on its own cloud computer after you close it. It asks for approval before it sends, pays, signs, or deletes anything. It's waitlist-only for US Pro and Max users.
*Why builders care:* Its background checks count against your plan's usage limits, which is a useful model for how to budget an always-on agent of your own.
[source](https://claude.com/resources/articles/claude-duet)

[CODING]
**3. Recursive's Flint: a coding model that runs on your laptop**
Flint is a 40B mixture-of-experts model that uses about 2.5B parameters per token. Recursive reports 74.2% on SWE-bench Verified and more than 125 tokens/sec on an M4 Pro MacBook Pro. It's Apache 2.0 on Hugging Face and works with Ollama, LM Studio, llama.cpp and vLLM.
*Why builders care:* A private, offline coding agent with no usage bill. Compare it with the hosted options in our [coding agent guide](https://hotfixdaily.com/guides/which-ai-coding-agent/).
[source](https://recursive.com/updates/introducing-recursive-flint)

[GAME DEV]
**4. More than a third of Steam Next Fest games now use generative AI**
TheGamer's count of SteamDB data found 2,595 of the 7,145 games in October's Next Fest (over 36%) carry Steam's AI tag, up from just over 19% in June. Players are pushing back, and many of the top-charting demos are AI-free.
*Why builders care:* Disclosed AI use is now normal on Steam, and players are watching. Being clear about how you used it can help you stand out.
[source](https://www.thegamer.com/steam-next-fest-ai-usage-has-jumped-from-one-in-five-to-one-in-three/)

[REPO]
**5. Repo of the day: OPAL, an optimizer an agent rewrites mid-training**
From MIT researchers: wrap your PyTorch optimizer in one line, and a coding agent (Claude Code by default) watches the run and rewrites the update rule, schedules, and loss-spike guards as it trains. MIT-licensed, with a cost cap you set.
*Why builders care:* For a new task with no tuned recipe, the authors report it matches or beats the best off-the-shelf recipe across their image and language tests.
[source](https://github.com/xingjian-bai/opal)

---

### Hotfix of the Day
Match reasoning effort to the step. On MiniMax-M3.1-Flash, `effort` defaults to `max` if you leave it out. Set it to `low` for routing, classification, and simple tool calls, and keep `high` or `max` for planning and debugging. Check what your provider defaults to.
[source](https://platform.minimax.io/docs/guides/text-generation)

## Hotfix Daily #1: Mercury 3, Voxtral 3, Beacon and more
URL: https://hotfixdaily.com/issues/001/ · Date: 2026-10-21



**Issue #1 · Wednesday, Oct 21, 2026**

Five things from the last 48 hours worth your attention if you build with AI. No fluff.

[Read this issue on the web](https://hotfixdaily.com/issues/001/) · [Sponsor Hotfix Daily](https://hotfixdaily.com/sponsor/)

---

[MODEL]
**1. Inception ships Mercury 3, a diffusion model built for speed**
Mercury 3 drafts the whole response at once and then refines it, instead of writing one token at a time. On Inception's own benchmarks it beat GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5 on 8 of 12 tests at 1,068 tokens/sec, and it has a 1M-token context. No one outside the company has published results yet.
*Why builders care:* It is on OpenRouter and Vercel, and OpenAI-API code needs only minor changes, so testing it is cheap.
[source](https://siliconangle.com/2026/10/20/inception-says-mercury-3-beats-gpt-6-luna-and-claude-haiku-5-5-at-up-to-8x-the-speed/)

[AGENTS]
**2. Mistral launches Voxtral 3 and a voice agent SDK**
New speech-to-text and text-to-speech models plus an SDK built on LiveKit. It runs listening, reasoning, tool calls, and speech as one streaming pipeline, and Mistral says each turn finishes in under a second. It works over WebRTC in browsers and over SIP for phone calls.
*Why builders care:* Voice agents used to mean wiring three vendors together. Now it's one SDK priced per minute, and you can still swap out the LLM.
[source](https://mistral.ai/news/voxtral-3/)

[CODING]
**3. Beacon: shared memory for your coding agents**
Asymptote Labs raised a $5.5M seed round for Beacon, an MIT-licensed open-source layer. It records sessions across Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and 20+ other agent tools, and it lets lessons from earlier sessions carry over instead of disappearing.
*Why builders care:* If you hop between Cursor and Claude Code, you can stop re-explaining your project to each one.
[source](https://www.asymptotelabs.ai/blog/asymptote-labs-raises-5-5m-seed-round)

[GAME DEV]
**4. Game studios use AI everywhere, but not deeply**
Vivrato interviewed 101 studio leaders: 94% use AI in at least one production stage, yet 52% rate how deeply it's built into their pipeline at 3/10 or lower. European studios reported deeper adoption than North American ones.
*Why builders care:* The gap is in the pipeline. Studios have picked up AI tools but haven't built them into how they work, and that's an opening for tools that fit real game dev workflows.
[source](https://gamesbeat.com/adam-boyes-vivrato-issues-report-based-on-101-game-leaders-views-on-ai-in-gaming-exclusive/)

[REPO]
**5. Repo of the day: Google's Harness²**
This trending open-source framework (Apache 2.0) improves the setup around an agent while the agent works: prompts, memory, tools, skills, and subagents. The model itself stays the same. Google reports gains of up to 11.5 points on WorkBuddy-Bench. It supports OpenCode and Codex as executors.
*Why builders care:* You can get better results by improving the setup around your model, without switching to a new one.
[source](https://github.com/google-research/harness2)

---

### Hotfix of the Day
Before you accept "done" from your coding agent, make it **show proof**: run the tests, the build, or a screenshot. Then have a fresh-context subagent review the diff. The Claude Code team says that's the first layer of their review process. From June to September, their merged PRs more than doubled while the share needing reverts fell by over 40%. Put your run-able checks in a short `CLAUDE.md` (or `.cursorrules`).
[source](https://claude.dev/blog/solving-code-review-at-anthropic/)
